indexes.conf\t<index_name>\tcoldPath.live_evidence: Throwaway btool tree accepted coldPath = volume:probe_vol/probe_two/colddb and coldPath = /data/splunkidx/probe_three/colddb, both read back verbatim, btool check exit 0; both fail the criterion's pattern. On the live instance every shipped index carries coldPath = $SPLUNK_DB/<name>/colddb from /opt/splunk/etc/system/default/indexes.conf, on the same device as /opt/splunk/etc.
indexes.conf\t<index_name>\tcoldPath.notes: Same defect as homePath, and sharper here: the vendor's own recommended multi-partition layout puts cold buckets on a separate array, which is expressed either as a literal path or as a volume reference - and the criterion rejects both while accepting the single-partition default. Requiring ^\$SPLUNK_DB/ on coldPath actively discourages the configuration the requirement is asking for.
indexes.conf\t<index_name>\tcoldPath.vendor_says: The 10.4.2 indexes.conf.spec shipped with the product (line 505): "An absolute path that contains the colddbs for the index"; "Best practice is to specify the path with the following syntax: coldPath = $SPLUNK_DB/$_index_name/colddb"; "Can contain a volume reference (see volume section below) in place of $SPLUNK_DB." Required. Vendor 10.4 "Use multiple partitions for index data" describes the common layout as hot and warm buckets on the local machine and cold buckets "on a separate array of disks suitable for longer term storage" - that is, coldPath is the path most likely to be legitimately pointed off $SPLUNK_DB.

indexes.conf\t<index_name>\thomePath.correction: Remove the condition. Whether index data sits on a partition separate from the Splunk system files is a filesystem property that no indexes.conf value expresses, so it belongs in external_dependencies. If an application-layer condition is wanted, it belongs on splunk-launch.conf SPLUNK_DB (set, and resolving outside $SPLUNK_HOME), not on an indexes.conf path.
indexes.conf\t<index_name>\thomePath.live_evidence: In a throwaway btool tree, three forms were all accepted and read back verbatim with btool check exit 0: $SPLUNK_DB/probe_one/db, volume:probe_vol/probe_two/db, and /data/splunkidx/probe_three/db. The last two fail the criterion's ^\$SPLUNK_DB/ pattern. On the live instance SPLUNK_DB is commented out in /opt/splunk/etc/splunk-launch.conf (line 13), so it resolves to $SPLUNK_HOME/var/lib/splunk; stat -c '%d' reports device 64513 for both /opt/splunk/etc and /opt/splunk/var/lib/splunk - the same partition - while every shipped index carries homePath = $SPLUNK_DB/<name>/db and therefore satisfies the criterion.
indexes.conf\t<index_name>\thomePath.notes: The criterion is wrong in both directions, and the live instance demonstrates each. It PASSES here, where index data and system files share one device, because $SPLUNK_DB is left at its default inside the installation tree - so meeting the condition does not satisfy the requirement. And it would FAIL a configuration that does satisfy the requirement: a literal absolute path on a separate array, and a volume reference, which the product's own 10.4.2 spec explicitly permits in place of $SPLUNK_DB and which is Splunk's recommended way to control storage location. Vendor documentation also states that for SmartStore indexes "The home path and cold path of each index must point to the same partition", which is at odds with the requirement's framing. Note also that this condition is not among the failing conditions for SRG-APP-000233-WSR-000146: running the project's own assess/bin/evaluate.sh against the latest results, the only failing conditions are four splunk-launch.conf SPLUNK_DB checks written against TLS version patterns (matches tls1\.2, not_matches ...ssl3, tls1\.0, tls1\.1). SPLUNK_DB is a filesystem path; those four can never be satisfied and appear cross-contaminated from a TLS rule.
indexes.conf\t<index_name>\thomePath.vendor_says: The 10.4.2 indexes.conf.spec shipped with the product (line 471) states: "An absolute path that contains the hot and warm buckets for the index"; "Best practice is to specify the path with the following syntax: homePath = $SPLUNK_DB/$_index_name/db"; and, decisively, "Can contain a volume reference (see volume section below) in place of $SPLUNK_DB." Required - splunkd does not start if an index lacks a valid homePath. Vendor 10.4 "Use multiple partitions for index data": "The indexer can use multiple partitions for its index data", paths are set per index, and the topic does not apply to SmartStore indexes. The 10.4 "Configure index storage" page states "Do not use environment variables in index paths" with SPLUNK_DB as the one exception.

indexes.conf\t<index_name>\tthawedPath.correction: Remove the condition; the partition determination belongs in external_dependencies, as described for homePath.
indexes.conf\t<index_name>\tthawedPath.live_evidence: Throwaway btool tree accepted thawedPath = /data/splunkidx/probe_three/thaweddb, read back verbatim, btool check exit 0; it fails the criterion's pattern. Live instance: every shipped index carries thawedPath = $SPLUNK_DB/<name>/thaweddb from system/default, on the same device as /opt/splunk/etc, so the criterion passes while the requirement is unmet.
indexes.conf\t<index_name>\tthawedPath.notes: The volume counter-example does not apply here - the spec forbids a volume reference in thawedPath, so the criterion's rationale is correct on that narrow point. The fatal defect is the other one: ^\$SPLUNK_DB/ is satisfied by the stock single-partition install and rejects a literal absolute path on a separate partition, which is exactly what the requirement asks for. The criterion's stated reasoning, that expressing the path relative to the index root "is what lets the data follow the separate partition", is the inversion: $SPLUNK_DB resolves inside $SPLUNK_HOME unless splunk-launch.conf says otherwise, and on this instance it is commented out.
indexes.conf\t<index_name>\tthawedPath.vendor_says: The 10.4.2 indexes.conf.spec shipped with the product (line 527): "An absolute path that contains the thawed (resurrected) databases for the index"; "CANNOT contain a volume reference"; "Path must be writable"; "Required. Splunkd does not start if an index lacks a valid thawedPath." The 10.4 "Configure index storage" page lists thawedPath as "The path that contains any thawed buckets. (Required.)" and applies the no-environment-variables rule, SPLUNK_DB excepted, to it.

indexes.conf\tvolume:<volume_name>\tremo.correction: Remove the unconditional condition. Make it conditional on a remote volume existing and, where one does, write it per volume with the vocabulary enumerated: indexes.conf [volume:<the deployment's actual volume name>] remote.s3.encryption in sse-s3|sse-kms|sse-c|cse. Move encryption of locally stored index data to external_dependencies.
indexes.conf\tvolume:<volume_name>\tremo.live_evidence: The live instance has no remote storage at all: btool indexes list --debug matched zero remote.path or remote.s3.* lines, and the only volume stanza is [volume:_splunk_summaries] with path = $SPLUNK_DB, a local path. So the setting has nothing to act on here. Operand permissiveness measured in a throwaway btool tree: a volume stanza carrying remote.s3.encryption = sse3, a value outside the documented list, was read back verbatim and splunk btool check printed nothing and exited 0.
indexes.conf\tvolume:<volume_name>\tremo.notes: Three separate defects. (1) The condition can never be satisfied as written. The collector compares stanzas literally, so volume:<volume_name> matches no real stanza and the key is recorded absent on every instance regardless of configuration - the same class of defect as the authorize.conf role_<roleName> criterion. Every indexes.conf stanza in the inventory is empty or a placeholder (<index>, <index name>, <index_name>, volume:<name>, volume:<volume_name>); the flattened evidence map holds real names such as _audit and volume:_splunk_summaries, so a literal stanza does resolve. (2) The operand is too permissive: not_equals none passes any typo, and nothing in the collection path validates it - btool check accepted sse3 silently. (3) The condition is applied to a deployment with no remote store. On a non-SmartStore indexer, data at rest sits on local disk and Splunk Enterprise offers no application setting that encrypts it; that is host or storage-platform encryption and belongs in external_dependencies, not in a condition. As a secondary point, sse-s3, sse-kms and sse-c are encryption performed by the object store rather than by Splunk, so even when met the condition evidences the provider's algorithm, not the application's.
indexes.conf\tvolume:<volume_name>\tremo.vendor_says: Vendor 10.4 "SmartStore on S3 security strategies": the scheme is set "under the [volume:<volume_name>] stanza for that volume"; values remote.s3.encryption = sse-s3 | sse-kms | sse-c | cse | none; "Choosing the encryption method is a one-time decision. You cannot change the encryption method later"; enabling it "you do not cause data that is already on the volume to be encrypted", and disabling leaves existing encrypted data unusable. The 10.4 indexes.conf reference gives the same value list and "Default: none". The setting governs only a SmartStore remote object store; it has no bearing on local index storage.

inputs.conf\t\tindex.correction: Remove the condition. The objective - automatic aggregation of account-action events for each in-scope device - is not decidable from inputs.conf and belongs in external_dependencies, since the scope of coverage is organization-defined. If a machine condition is wanted for the application's share, it is the existence of a receiving listener, as corrected for [splunktcp].
inputs.conf\t\tindex.live_evidence: btool inputs list --debug shows index = default supplied from etc/system/default/inputs.conf for effectively every stanza on the instance, including [SSL], [splunktcp], [http] and [splunktcp-ssl://9997]. With no stanza named, the collector resolved the condition to inputs.conf / (empty stanza) / index / declared / present / default, so it passes - as it would on any install.
inputs.conf\t\tindex.notes: The condition carries no stanza at all, and index has a documented default and is set from the shipped default file for every input, so non_empty is true on every install and separates nothing. It also does not test what the requirement asks: naming a destination index says nothing about whether account-action events from in-scope devices are being aggregated. This requirement is currently open because of its eventtypes.conf condition, not this one, so correcting it changes no status - but it leaves one fewer condition that cannot fail.
inputs.conf\t\tindex.vendor_says: inputs.conf.spec 10.4.2 lines 93-97, in the global settings section that opens the file: "index = <string> * Sets the index to store events from this input. * Primarily used to specify the index to store events that come in through this input stanza. * Default: main (or whatever you have set as your default index)." The setting recurs with stanza-specific wording for scripted inputs (line 1464) and for the fschange input (line 1520). It is an ordinary per-input destination setting, not a selector for any category of event.

inputs.conf\tSSL\trequireClientCert.correction: inputs.conf [splunktcp-ssl:<port>] requireClientCert in true|1, with [SSL] accepted as an equivalent placement and the stanza resolved against the stanzas that actually exist
inputs.conf\tSSL\trequireClientCert.live_evidence: btool inputs list --debug shows requireClientCert = true on [splunktcp-ssl://9997] and nothing under [SSL]; the assessment TSV reports inputs.conf [SSL] requireClientCert absent. metrics.log shows 931 accepted connections, all cookedSSL with ssl=true, so the port-level setting is in force and the receiver is demanding the forwarder certificate.
inputs.conf\tSSL\trequireClientCert.notes: Same placement fault as serverCert: a receiver that does require client certificates is reported as not requiring them, because the setting is on the port stanza rather than [SSL]. There is a second, subtler point the documentation makes: under [SSL] this setting is described as governing HTTPS clients connecting to splunkd generally - distributed search, deployment clients, indexer-to-indexer - so moving it to [SSL] widens its effect well past the data receiver the requirement is about, while the per-port [splunktcp-ssl:<port>] setting is the one that makes this receiver demand the forwarder certificate. Note also that the documented default is conditional, false with self-signed or third-party certificates and true with the shipped default certificates, so no criterion may assume a default state for this setting.
inputs.conf\tSSL\trequireClientCert.vendor_says: inputs.conf.spec 10.4.2 lines 1019-1037 ([SSL]): "Whether or not an HTTPS client which connects to a splunkd server must possess a certificate that a certificate authority signed to complete the connection. * Multiple services can use this setting, including but not limited to distributed search and distributed deployment clients... * Default (if using self-signed and third-party certificates): false * Default (if using the default certificates; overrides the existing \"false\" setting): true". Also declared under [splunktcp-ssl:<port>] at line 928.

inputs.conf\tSSL; splunktcp-ssl:<port>\t.live_evidence: btool inputs list --debug shows [SSL] cipherSuite set in etc/system/default/inputs.conf to ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-SHA256, and the assessment TSV records that same value as present. Running the criterion's pattern against it matches; the pattern also rejects DEFAULT, HIGH:!aNULL and a comma-separated list, and accepts TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256.
inputs.conf\tSSL; splunktcp-ssl:<port>\t.notes: The setting exists in both stanzas, the pattern is inside the accepted vocabulary, and it does what the rationale claims: it admits only AES with SHA-2 suites in Splunk's colon-separated OpenSSL form and rejects the class strings. The rationale is nonetheless wrong on one point of fact that only the instance settles - it says an unset value falls back to the OpenSSL default string, but on a stock 10.4.2 install the setting is never unset, because etc/system/default/inputs.conf supplies an explicit AES/GCM list that already satisfies the pattern. So this condition contributes no finding on a stock install; it is a guard against an operator replacing the default with something weaker. One deliberate exclusion worth recording: the pattern rejects TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which is correct for an AES-only reading of the requirement but will fail a TLS 1.3 configuration that offers ChaCha20.

See the 'cipherSuite' setting in the $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/default/inputs.conf file for the current default." Also declared under [splunktcp-ssl:<port>] at line 930.

inputs.conf\tSSL; splunktcp-ssl:<port>\t.live_evidence: btool inputs list --debug shows the real receiving stanza [splunktcp-ssl://9997] from an app default with serverCert = /opt/splunk/etc/auth/labcerts/epo-uat-indexer-combined.pem, requireClientCert = true, sslVersions = tls1.2, disabled = 0. splunkd.log: "TcpInputProc [2412 TcpListener] - Creating fwd data Acceptor for IPv4 port 9997 with SSL". metrics.log: 931 group=tcpin_connections records, every one connectionType=cookedSSL with ssl=true from hostname=epo-uat-hf, destPort=9997. Yet the assessment TSV reports inputs.conf serverCert absent for stanza splunktcp-ssl:<port> (three requirements), for stanza splunktcp-ssl (one), and for stanza SSL (two).
inputs.conf\tSSL; splunktcp-ssl:<port>\t.notes: This is the clearest false finding in the file, and only a live run shows it. The receiver is doing mutual TLS on port 9997 with a PEM certificate, 931 connections accepted as cookedSSL - and both criterion forms report the certificate absent. Cause: the criterion names a stanza that is a specification placeholder, and the collector matches it as a literal string, so neither "splunktcp-ssl:<port>" nor "SSL" ever matches the real stanza name "splunktcp-ssl://9997". The placeholder resolution in evaluate.sh cannot recover it either, because its index is built only from rows the criteria themselves requested, and every such row is already keyed to a placeholder that resolved to absent. Separately, requiring the certificate specifically under [SSL] over-constrains placement: the vendor states plainly that per-port stanzas carry any setting that deviates from the global one, and the vendor's own worked example writes the certificate under [SSL] and the port as the bare stanza [splunktcp-ssl:9996]. Note the two real-world stanza spellings, [splunktcp-ssl:9996] (the vendor example) and [splunktcp-ssl://9997] (this instance); any corrected criterion must match both.

outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslPasswor.notes: The setting exists and the operand is well formed, but the condition does not test what any of the three requirements ask. sslPassword unlocks a local key file; it neither authenticates the source nor protects anything in transit. So a forwarder with a correctly installed, file-permission-protected unencrypted key presents a valid client certificate over TLS and is marked open. The condition is faithful to SPLK-CL-000460 fix text, which lists sslPassword beside clientCert - that is where it came from - but the benchmark's fix text is an example configuration, not a requirement that the key be encrypted. Drop the condition on all three requirements; clientCert already carries the mutual-authentication half and the TLS conditions carry the transport half. If key protection is wanted it is a requirement about the key file, which belongs in external_dependencies - the key's permissions and encryption are not outputs.conf settings.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslPasswor.vendor_says: The 10.4 reference: "The password associated with the Certificate Authority certificate (CAcert)", "The default Splunk CAcert uses the password 'password'", no default. The 10.4 forwarding-TLS page marks the setting optional, describes it as the private key password, says not to configure it when no password was set on the private key, and notes that a cleartext value in outputs.conf is encrypted on restart. The spec's GLOBAL SETTINGS preamble warns that sslPassword in [default] "may remain readable to attackers".

outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslRootCAP.live_evidence: btool --dir check accepts sslRootCAPath in both [tcpout] and [tcpout:g1], and a merged listing returns it, so the deprecated setting is still live and still capable of introducing a second anchor set. Not set anywhere in outputs.conf on the running instance, so the absent condition passes. The instance's single trust store is set where the vendor says it should be: etc/system/local/server.conf sslRootCAPath = /opt/splunk/etc/auth/labcerts/ca.pem.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslRootCAP.notes: The setting exists under that name in that stanza, it is deprecated in favour of the server.conf setting, and the vendor's "Used only if 'sslRootCAPath' in server.conf is not set" is exactly the mechanism the rationale relies on - requiring it absent keeps one organization-managed trust store rather than a per-output second set of anchors, which is what SRG-APP-000910-AU-000390 asks. The operator is also the right one for the evaluator: absent is the only operator in evaluate.sh that treats a missing key as a pass, so this condition reads correctly on an instance where the key is simply not there. This condition already passes; SRG-APP-000910-AU-000390 is open on its server.conf conditions, not this one.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslRootCAP.vendor_says: The 10.4 reference: "The full path to the root Certificate Authority (CA) certificate store", "DEPRECATED", "Use the 'server.conf/[sslConfig]/sslRootCAPath' setting instead", "Used only if 'sslRootCAPath' in server.conf is not set", "The <path> must refer to a PEM format file containing one or more root CA certificates concatenated together", no default.

outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslVerifyS.live_evidence: btool --dir check accepts sslVerifyServerCert in both [tcpout] and [tcpout:g1]; a merged listing returns sslVerifyServerCert = true. Not set in any layer on the running instance, so the effective value is the documented default false.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslVerifyS.notes: The setting exists where the criterion says, the default is false so the finding is real rather than an artifact of an already-compliant default, and what the setting does - validating the receiver's certificate and its common and alternate names - is what the rationale claims. Both operand spellings in the file resolve the same way: `matches ^(1|true)$` on SRG-APP-000334-WSR-000024 and `in 1|true` on the other two. Prefer `in 1|true` for consistency. One caveat the vendor raises and the criteria do not: a receiver certificate sharing a Common Name with its CA fails this check, so enabling it can break a working deployment - that belongs in the fix text, not the criterion.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslVerifyS.vendor_says: The 10.4 reference: "Serves as an additional step for authenticating your indexers", "A value of 'true' ensures that the server you are connecting to has a valid SSL certificate", "Both the common name and the alternate name of the server are then checked for a match", "NOTE: Certificates with the same Common Name as the CA's certificate will fail this check", Default: false. The 10.4 forwarding-TLS page adds that sslCommonNameToCheck requires sslVerifyServerCert to be true before the forwarder performs the verification, and sets it to true in its own example.

outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslVersion.correction: outputs.conf [tcpout:<target_group>] sslVersions not_matches (^|[ ,])(\*|tls1\.0|tls1\.1|ssl3|tls)([ ,]|$)  AND  outputs.conf [tcpout:<target_group>] sslVersions matches tls1\.[23]
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslVersion.live_evidence: /opt/splunk/etc/system/default/outputs.conf on the running 10.4.2 instance sets `sslVersions = tls1.2, tls1.3`, which is what btool outputs list --debug resolves for [tcpout] - the vendor's own shipped default is exactly the value this condition fails. btool --dir check accepts sslVersions in [tcpout] and [tcpout:g1] but does not validate the value: it accepted sslVersions = tls9.9 without complaint. tls1.2 is live-proven to be an accepted operand elsewhere on this instance - etc/system/local/server.conf carries sslVersions = tls1.2 and the instance is running.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslVersion.notes: `equals tls1.2` marks Splunk 10.4.2's own shipped default, tls1.2 and tls1.3, as non-compliant, and remediating it means turning TLS 1.3 off to satisfy a requirement that asks for an approved TLS version. The operand is an 8.x value: SPLK-CL-000430 was written when tls1.3 did not exist in the product, and its fix text is conditional in the first place - "If the following lines do not exist, then the settings are compliant." The corrected pair keeps what the requirement actually needs - no tls1.0, no tls1.1, no bare wildcard that reaches them, and at least one of tls1.2 or tls1.3 - and is the same shape as the SRG's intent. Both patterns were run through POSIX ERE in awk, the engine evaluate.sh uses, and behave correctly on tls1.2, "tls1.2, tls1.3", tls1.3, -tls1.3 (pass) and on *, tls, tls1.1, "tls1.0, tls1.2", "tls1.2, tls1.1" (fail); neither uses a lookaround, so neither trips evaluate.sh's PCRE guard. The same correction applies to the sibling sslVersions conditions on web.conf, server.conf, inputs.conf and alert_actions.conf, which carry the same `equals tls1.2` operand against the same 10.4 default.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tsslVersion.vendor_says: The 10.4 reference: "The versions available are 'tls1.0', 'tls1.1', 'tls1.2', and 'tls1.3'", "*" selects all supported versions, "tls" selects all versions tls1.0 or newer, a "-" prefix removes a version, SSL 2 and 3 are always disabled, and "The default can vary. See the 'sslVersions' setting in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/default/outputs.conf". The TLS version page: "Version 1.3 of the TLS protocol is available starting in Splunk Enterprise version 10.4.0", TLS 1.3 is "Active alongside TLS 1.2 by default when you upgrade to version 10.4.0 or higher", TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are off by default at 10.4.0 and higher, and the cipher page states "The default sslVersions setting for Splunk configuration files changes from tls1.2 to tls1.2,tls1.3."

outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tuseACK.live_evidence: btool --dir check accepts useACK in [tcpout], [tcpout:g1] and - contrary to the spec's "You cannot set it for individual servers" - in [tcpout-server://10.0.0.1:9997], so btool does not enforce that restriction. It does not validate the value either: useACK = banana was accepted. On the running instance useACK = false resolves from system/default, the documented default.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tuseACK.notes: The setting exists and the operand is fine, but it does not do what the requirement asks. SRG-APP-000441-WSR-000181 is about maintaining confidentiality and integrity of information during preparation for transmission. Indexer acknowledgment is a delivery guarantee: the vendor describes it as preventing loss of data, and it protects nothing in the output queue from disclosure or modification - it makes data in that queue live longer, raises the queue memory ceiling from 500KB to 28MB, and the vendor warns it can cause the same block to be indexed twice. It belongs to availability and to the off-load requirements, not to SC-8. Drop it from SRG-APP-000441-WSR-000181; the clientCert, useSSL, sslVersions and sslVerifyServerCert conditions on that requirement are the ones that bear on it. Worth carrying forward as a condition on SRG-APP-000515-AU-000110, where reliable off-load is the point.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tuseACK.vendor_says: The 10.4 reference heads the section "Indexer acknowledgment ensures that forwarded data is reliably delivered to the receiver" and says useACK is "an optional capability on forwarders that helps prevent loss of data when sending data to an indexer"; true "means the forwarder retains a copy of each sent event until the receiving system sends an acknowledgment" and resends to an alternative receiver otherwise; "the maximum memory used for the outbound data queues increases significantly by default (500KB -> 28MB)"; settable at [tcpout] or [tcpout:<target_group>] but not per server; Default: false. The 10.4 cluster guide frames it as guarding against data loss and notes duplicates are possible when an acknowledgment is lost after the data was written.

outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tuseClientS.live_evidence: btool --dir check accepts the key in both stanzas. On the running instance btool outputs list --debug resolves useClientSSLCompression = true for [tcpout] from /opt/splunk/etc/system/default/outputs.conf - the documented default, and non-compliant. No app or local layer overrides it: there is no etc/system/local/outputs.conf, and the three app copies (SplunkForwarder and SplunkLightForwarder, both state = disabled, plus SplunkDeploymentServerConfig) set only forwardedindex and maxQueueSize. Compression is genuinely available: the bundled OpenSSL was built with -DZLIB and its s_client offers -comp. The enabling half is also present - server.conf default allowSslCompression = true.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tuseClientS.notes: The setting exists under that name, the operand is within the boolean vocabulary, the default is true so the finding is real, and setting it false does what the rationale claims. Two things to record rather than change. First, the condition is only partly effective at 10.4: with the default sslVersions = tls1.2, tls1.3 a TLS 1.3 session cannot compress regardless, so the setting matters only on the TLS 1.2 sessions the same default still permits. Second, the requirement text is about web server session cookies, and this is the forwarder-to-indexer S2S channel, which carries no cookies - the condition is defensible as the same compression-oracle vulnerability class, but the mapping is a stretch and should be stated. Separately, the finding's recorded observation for this condition reads "is false", which the current instance does not support: the live value is true. Whatever state that observation came from, it is not epo-uat-indexer as it stands now.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<group>\tuseClientS.vendor_says: The 10.4 reference: "Whether or not compression on TLS/SSL connections is enabled", "Server-side compression in splunkd is on by default. Configuring this setting on the client side enables compression between both server and client", "If server-side compression is off, this client-side setting has no effect", "SSL compression is not supported for TLS 1.3", Default: true. The 10.4 cipher page: the outputs.conf setting "has no effect for TLS 1.3 connections because TLS 1.3 does not support SSL compression."

outputs.conf\ttcpout:<target_group>\tser.live_evidence: btool --dir check accepts server in [tcpout:g1]; a merged listing of that stanza returns server = 10.0.0.1:9997 alongside indexerDiscovery, clientCert, sslRootCAPath, sslVerifyServerCert and useSSL. On the running instance no [tcpout:*] stanza exists in any layer, so the observation "not set" is correct.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<target_group>\tser.notes: The setting exists under that exact name in that stanza, the operator matches what the vendor says the setting holds, and a populated value is what names the aggregation target - this is the right condition for all five requirements, and it is the correction for SRG-APP-000515-AU-000110's [tcpout] spelling. One real alternative remains open: the vendor states server is required only when indexerDiscovery is not set, so a cluster forwarder using indexer discovery satisfies the requirement with no server list. The assessment already records that alternative in external_dependencies for SRG-APP-000358-WSR-000063, which is the right place for it given the evaluator has no disjunction.
outputs.conf\ttcpout:<target_group>\tser.vendor_says: Under [tcpout:<target_group>]: "A comma-separated list of one or more systems to send data to over a TCP socket", each element "either an IP address or a hostname and a port number", "Required if the 'indexerDiscovery' setting is not set", and "Typically used to specify receiving Splunk systems, although you can use it to send data to non-Splunk systems (see the 'sendCookedData' setting)." No default.

savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tactio.correction: Drop the condition. The delivered form of a report is organization-defined and is spread across five switches plus alert_actions.conf, so it belongs in external_dependencies, not in a condition on one key.
savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tactio.live_evidence: Probe: action.email.sendpdf = 1 accepted and read back as 1; = true read back as 'true'; = 3 also accepted with btool check exiting 0. `btool savedsearches list --debug | grep -c 'action.email.sendpdf'` -> 0: absent from the entire effective configuration, so 'present' is non-vacuous here, unlike the dispatch and schedule_window cases.
savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tactio.notes: The rationale says the criterion is 'that the report states its form rather than a particular value'. The operator makes that a no-op: 'present' is satisfied by writing action.email.sendpdf = 0, which is byte-for-byte the documented default and changes nothing about the delivered report. A condition that can be met by writing a line with no effect is not a control. Two further problems the documentation establishes: the default can be supplied by alert_actions.conf, so savedsearches.conf alone cannot determine the form; and PDF is one of five form switches, so singling it out does not test 'the form' at all.
savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tactio.vendor_says: action.email.sendpdf = [1|0]. 'Specify whether to send results as a PDF file.' 'Default: 0 (false) (or the sendpdf setting in the alert_actions.conf file)'. Live 10.4.2 spec line 418, identical text. The file carries four sibling form switches: action.email.inline (399), .sendcsv (405), .sendpng (423), .sendresults (428). There is no action.email.format in savedsearches.conf 10.4.2.

savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\talert.correction: Drop the condition. If a trigger must be asserted at all, the condition is a disjunction: savedsearches.conf [*] alert_condition non_empty OR counttype in 'number of events|number of hosts|number of sources|custom' with relation and quantity set. A bare alert_condition non_empty must not be a condition.

Decisive counter-measurement: `grep -cE '^alert_condition = .+'` -> 0 of 182 stanzas, while `grep -cE '^counttype = (number of|custom)'`, `^relation = .+` and `^quantity = .+` each return 20. Splunk's own shipped DMC alerts trigger the other way - 'DMC Alert - Missing forwarders' reads counttype = number of events, relation = greater than, quantity = 0, enableSched = 1, alert_condition = (empty).
savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\talert.notes: This criterion reports a finding against 20 working alerts that Splunk ships in the product. The assessment reached exactly this conclusion already and applied it unevenly: the citation text for SRG-APP-000293-AU-000430 and -000294-AU-000440 says alert_condition non_empty 'reports a finding against a working alert' because counttype with relation and quantity is the other form, and the condition was removed from those two - while the identical condition survived in these four. Two of the four also rest on observations that are not savedsearches.conf values ('is 5000', 'is web_access.log').
savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\talert.vendor_says: alert_condition = <search string>. 'Contains a conditional search that is evaluated against the results of the saved search. Alerts are triggered if the specified search yields a non-empty search result list.' 'Default: empty string'. Live 10.4.2 spec line 305, identical text. The alerting manual describes the same thing in UI terms: 'Trigger conditions work as a secondary search to evaluate the alert's initial search results', with 'Built-in result and field count options or a custom triggering condition' - two alternatives, not one.

savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tcount.correction: Drop the condition. 'custom' is one of five values, not a prerequisite for alert_condition, and the vendor documents no dependency between them in 10.4.2.
savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tcount.live_evidence: Probe: counttype = custom accepted and read back verbatim; counttype = bogusvalue also accepted with btool check exiting 0, so btool cannot validate this vocabulary. `grep -cE '^counttype = custom$'` -> 0 of 182 stanzas; `grep -cE '^counttype = (number of|custom)'` -> 20, all of them 'number of ...' forms paired with relation and quantity. `grep -n -i 'alert_condition' savedsearches.conf.spec` -> one hit, line 305, with no reference to counttype.
savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tcount.notes: The operand 'custom' is inside the accepted vocabulary, so the criterion is satisfiable - but the rationale behind it is not supported by any vendor source I could find. It claims 'custom is the value under which the alert fires on the stated alert_condition rather than on every run'. The 10.4.2 spec says alert_condition triggers an alert whenever its search 'yields a non-empty search result list', unconditionally, with no mention of counttype. Older vendor spec text went the opposite way ('If you specify an alert_condition, do not set counttype, relation, or quantity'), a Splunk staff answer confirmed it and said earlier documentation had been corrected - and 10.4.2 contains neither sentence. I could not fetch that community thread directly (403), so I am reporting it as a search-level finding, not a quote I verified. What I did verify on the instance settles it anyway: 20 of Splunk's own shipped alerts set counttype to a 'number of ...' value and leave alert_condition empty, so requiring counttype = custom alongside alert_condition describes a pairing the product neither requires nor uses.
savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tcount.vendor_says: counttype = number of events | number of hosts | number of sources | custom | always. 'Set the type of count for alerting.' 'Used with the relation and quantity settings.' 'NOTE: If you specify "always," do not set relation or quantity.' 'Default: always'. Live 10.4.2 spec line 284, identical text. Nothing in the 10.4 or 10.0 entry for counttype or for alert_condition ties the two settings together in either direction.

savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tdispa.correction: savedsearches.conf [*] dispatch.earliest_time non_empty  -- replaces the 'present' operator in SRG-APP-000181-AU-000200, SRG-APP-000366-AU-000220 and SRG-APP-000765-AU-000160; SRG-APP-000368-AU-000240 and SRG-APP-000775-AU-000180 already use non_empty and need only the stanza correction.

A probe stanza with dispatch.earliest_time = -24h was accepted and read back verbatim; so was dispatch.earliest_time = ThisIsNotATime, with btool check exiting 0.

'present' is the wrong one and measurably vacuous - the shipped default makes the key present with an empty value, which bounds nothing, contradicting the rationale's own words that the window 'must be stated rather than left unbounded'. Do NOT simply substitute non_empty: that would fail 161 of the 182 saved searches Splunk itself ships. If a bound is genuinely required, the condition is savedsearches.conf [*] dispatch.latest_time non_empty and it must be justified against the 161 counter-examples first.

I could not confirm from vendor documentation what an empty dispatch.latest_time resolves to - the spec states only 'Default: empty string' - so I will not assert that empty means 'to the present'. What is measured is that the overwhelming majority of the product's own saved searches leave it empty, which makes a non_empty requirement a finding-generator against working configuration. Whether an audit review report needs a stated closing bound is an organization-defined reporting-window question, not a product setting.

savedsearches.conf\t<stanza name>\tsched.correction: Drop the condition from both findings. It is a scheduler load-smoothing knob, not a reporting control, and nothing in either requirement reaches it.

server.conf\tgeneral\tinvalidateSessionT.vendor_says: 'invalidateSessionTokensOnLogout = <boolean>', 'Default: false'. server.conf\thttpServer\tmaxSockets.live_evidence: btool server list httpServer --debug: '$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/default/server.conf maxSockets = 0' - the vendor default, not a local setting. splunkd.log at startup: 'INFO ulimit - Limit: open files: 524288 files', so the effective ceiling the product computes here is 524288/3 = 174762 simultaneous connections, inside the documented 50..400000 clamp.
server.conf\thttpServer\tmaxSockets.notes: The operand is off by one class of value. 'min 1' flags 0, and 0 is the value at which the product enforces a computed limit; the unlimited case is a negative number, which 'min 0' catches and 'min 1' catches only incidentally. The assessor's own rationale states the correct semantics - 'default 0 = automatic limit, negative = no limits enforced' - and then writes min 1 anyway. With the correction the condition is satisfied by the shipped default, so the server.conf half of this finding is false. Writing a positive integer here to satisfy the criterion as it stands would lower the ceiling from 174762 to whatever number was invented, which works against the availability side of the requirement.
server.conf\thttpServer\tmaxSockets.vendor_says: Default: 0. 'The number of simultaneous HTTP connections that Splunk Enterprise accepts simultaneously.' 'If set to "0", Splunk Enterprise automatically sets maxSockets to one third of the maximum allowable open files on the host.' 'If this number is less than 50, it is set to 50.' 'If this number is greater than 400000, it is set to 400000.' 'If set to a negative number, no limit is enforced.' So 0 is a limit that the product computes; only a negative value is unlimited.

server.conf\thttpServer\tmaxThreads.live_evidence: btool server list httpServer --debug: '$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/default/server.conf maxThreads = 0' - vendor default. Same as maxSockets: 0 produces a computed limit, negative produces none.
server.conf\thttpServer\tmaxThreads.notes: Identical defect to maxSockets. Also note the product couples the two: maxThreads is silently reduced to maxSockets when it exceeds it, so a hand-written pair can be partly ignored.
server.conf\thttpServer\tmaxThreads.vendor_says: Default: 0. 'If set to 0, Splunk Enterprise automatically sets the limit to one third of the maximum allowable threads on the host.' 'If this number is less than 20, it is set to 20. If this number is greater than 150000, it is set to 150000.' 'If maxSockets is not negative and maxThreads is greater than maxSockets, then Splunk Enterprise sets maxThreads to be equal to maxSockets.' 'If set to a negative number, no limit is enforced.'

server.conf\tkvstore\tsslCRLPath.live_evidence: The key is in the 10.4.2 spec at line 5641 under [kvstore] (stanza header at line 5454) - the stanza the criterion names is correct, though the line number has moved from the 5392 the assessment cites in the 10.0.0 file. 'Splunkd uses the CRL file only in the following cases: When the Splunk platform instance is in Common Criteria mode (SPLUNK_COMMON_CRITERIA=1). 'The file that this setting value references must be in privacy-enhanced mail (PEM) format.' 'This setting is optional.' 'Default: empty string (no revocation list)'.

server.conf\tsslConfig\tallowSslCompress.live_evidence: btool server list sslConfig --debug: '$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/default/server.conf allowSslCompression = true' - the documented default, confirmed at line 169 of the shipped default file. Measured on the live handshake, however, nothing is compressed: 'splunk cmd openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8089' reports 'Compression: NONE' and 'Expansion: NONE' against OpenSSL 3.5.7 as shipped in 10.4.2.
server.conf\tsslConfig\tallowSslCompress.notes: The criterion is sound: the setting exists, the default is true, and the rationale describes TLS-layer compression correctly. The finding stands as a configuration finding. What the live test adds is that the exposure is nil on this build - the shipped OpenSSL negotiates no compression, and TLS 1.3 removes compression from the protocol - so the finding is a defense-in-depth configuration gap rather than an exploitable one, and the severity discussion should say so rather than imply cookies are being compressed today.
server.conf\tsslConfig\tallowSslCompress.vendor_says: 'allowSslCompression = <boolean>', 'Default: true'. 'Whether or not the server lets clients negotiate compression at the TLS layer.' 'A value of "false" means the server does not let clients negotiate TLS-layer data compression.' 'The app key value store (KV Store) service observes and uses this setting.'

server.conf\tsslConfig\tcaTrustStore.live_evidence: btool server list sslConfig --debug: '$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/default/server.conf caTrustStore = splunk' - confirmed at line 152 of the shipped default file, so the criterion's operand is the vendor default and the condition passes as shipped. The key is in the 10.4.2 spec at line 939 under [sslConfig]; [applicationsManagement] carries its own copy at line 1959.
server.conf\tsslConfig\tcaTrustStore.notes: The criterion is sound in vocabulary and in intent - splunk does confine validation to the curated store named by sslRootCAPath. But the operand equals the vendor default, so the condition can only fail on an instance where someone has changed it, and it cannot contribute to the two findings it sits under; both are Open on their certificateStatusValidationMethod and sslVerifyServerCert siblings. Two refinements: the vendor states the values are not case sensitive, so 'equals splunk' would reject a compliant 'Splunk', and a value of 'splunk,OS' is the real non-compliant case the requirement is aimed at - a not_matches test for OS would be more faithful than an exact match.

'A value of "splunk" means the platform only uses the certificate authority certificates in the trust store that the sslRootCAPath setting references.' 'A value of "OS" means the platform only uses the CA certificates in the trust store that the operating system on the instance defines.' 'Providing both values ("splunk,OS") means that the platform uses CA certificates within both the Splunk platform and operating system trust stores.' 'This values for this setting are not case sensitive.' caTrustStorePath has 'No default' and applies when caTrustStore is OS.

server.conf\tsslConfig\tcertificateStatu.live_evidence: The key is present in the 10.4.2 spec at line 1162 under the [sslConfig] stanza (header at line 744), so the stanza the criterion names is correct. server.conf\tsslConfig\tcertificateStatu.notes: Setting, stanza, operand and rationale all hold against 10.4.2 - this is the strongest criterion in the file, and the seven findings that rest on it stand.
